sources.news_title: Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on US companies that build AI data centers abroad
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday threatened "a tremendous tax" on U.S. companies that build artificial intelligence data centers abroad, highlighting a divide between a president who sees their expansion as critical to winning the AI race and an American public that is deeply skeptical of their benefits.
Briefing reporters at the White House shortly after his return from Asia, the president said the country was ahead of China in developing what he likes to call "super intelligence." But he warned it could fall behind if a growing political backlash puts the brakes on development of the data centers that are driving the AI boom.
"We're not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries," the president said. "If they do that, they can. But we're going to put a tremendous tax on them."
He contrasted his push to keep AI infrastructure in the U.S. with the foreign production of advanced computer chips, which he said had been "very destructive to our country."
You Might Also Like:Trump said he had not yet told his staff about his proposal to target data center development outside the U.S., and it was not immediately clear how it would be enforced.
His statements emphasized the gap between Trump's view of AI development and the views of most Americans and came less than three weeks after voter concerns about data centers contributed to a Republican wipe-out in the midterm elections.
About three-quarters of U.S. voters in this year's election said they opposed the construction of a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll.
In a survey taken over the summer, about 6 in 10 Americans said they supported limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans, according to the poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago.
You Might Also Like:
The same survey found that a majority of Americans are "extremely" or "very" concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.
With Democrats winning large majorities in both houses of Congress, a tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump - perhaps the industry's biggest champion - stalls any federal crackdown.
He suggested that data center concerns could be addressed through community negotiations with the tech companies seeking to build them. Tax breaks, reduced utility bills, money for teachers, direct payments to local residents all could be part of the talks.
"Make the deal," Trump said. "They have plenty of money. Take it."
The development of artificial intelligence is an important growth factor for data centers, but cloud computing services remain the dominant use of data centers in the U.S., industry officials say.
With host communities across the U.S. turning against the gargantuan data centers, America's technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets and shower more money on communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
Besides ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.
Companies also are making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values - all while maintaining that AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics.
"We want them to build it here," Trump said.
Many of the tech giants already have global footprints. Google has data centers in Asia and Europe.
Trump's threat to penalize companies that build data centers overseas reflects his view that the buildout is a boon for the U.S. economy. Most economists agree, but with caveats.
The largest high-tech firms are projected to spend as much as $1.8 trillion next year developing AI, mostly on data centers, economists at UBS estimate. The buildup has also boosted wages for some construction workers, particularly skilled contractors such as electricians, who are in short supply.
At the same time, most of the goods that power data centers - particularly semiconductors, but also materials such as copper - are imported, which offsets much of the economic gain.
On Thursday, the Republican-led Senate approved bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting reviews for power plants, transmission lines, and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation's energy supplies to meet surging demand and to lower electricity prices.
The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use and upgrades to the larger transmission network.
Trump praised the Senate bill, which now goes to the House: "It's going to cause tremendous amounts of new building," he said.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump could put billions of UK investment on ice with vow to punish tech giants financing overseas data centres
sources.text:
Donald Trump could put billions in UK investment on ice as he vowed to punish tech giants for funding overseas data centres.
The US President announced he would slap a “tremendous tax” on firms building huge AI hubs in other countries.
He was speaking from the White House briefing room just hours after returning from talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.
Despite the seemingly cordial meeting with the two leaders, Mr Trump warned that allowing American companies to build data centres abroad could put them in Beijing’s hands.
“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen,” he said
“And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” the US leader promised.
President Trump did not reveal details of this new approach but suggested firms that disobey him would face a “tremendous tax”.
“We want them to build it here,” he added.
If tech firms follow the White House’s new diktats and pull investment in data centres, it could risk billions of funding currently committed to the UK.
Tech giants Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle and CoreWeave, alongside developers like Equinix, CyrusOne, CloudHQ and QTS, have allocated huge sums to AI infrastructure in Britain.
The projects span the country, from Hertfordshire and Oxfordshire to Scotland and Northumberland.
Microsoft announced a £22billion investment in British AI infrastructure and operations between 2025 and 2028.
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS
Amazon Web Services (AWS) has committed £8billion between 2024 and 2028 to build, maintain and operate data centres in Britain. The investment is expected to support around 14,000 jobs, including roles in construction, engineering, telecommunications and facilities management.
Oracle has announced a separate $5billion (£3.9billion) investment over five years to expand its UK cloud infrastructure.
Google has already opened a new data centre at Waltham Cross in Hertfordshire, as part of a £5 billion UK investment over two years.
CoreWeave, an American cloud computing company specialising in AI, has committed £2.5billion to UK data-centre capacity and operations, in cooperation with Scottish firm DataVita, for a major facility north of the border.
Equinix has announced plans to spend £3.9billion on a new campus in Hertfordshire, forecast to create around 2,500 construction jobs and more than 200 permanent positions once fully operational.
American investment titan Blackstone has committed £10billion to a major AI data-centre campus at the former Blyth power station site in Northumberland.
CyrusOne has announced plans to invest £2.5billion in expanding its UK data-centre operations, with projects expected to come online from 2028.
CloudHQ, another American operator, is developing a £1.9billion data-centre campus near Didcot in Oxfordshire.
Vantage Data Centres has also announced an investment of up to £12billion to develop facilities in South Wales and west London.
Speaking in the Commons, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “important that communities see the benefits of AI and data centre investment.
“I can say from experience that the data centre can be the magnet that clusters in other investment over time; that needs to be remembered.
“This Government have a policy that AI growth zones will allow local authorities to retain 100% of business rate growth, so that they can benefit communities,” he told lawmakers.

sources.news_title: Can Trump Actually Impose a 'Tremendous Tax' on US Tech Firms Building AI Data Centres Abroad?
sources.text:
Can Trump Actually Impose a 'Tremendous Tax' on US Tech Firms Building AI Data Centres Abroad?
The president gave no rate or implementation details, raising questions about whether the proposed charge could be imposed without congressional action
The president threatened to penalise American companies that build AI data centres overseas, but he did not explain how the charge would work or identify the legal authority for imposing it
President Donald Trump threatened to impose a 'tremendous tax' on US technology companies that build artificial intelligence data centres abroad during a White House news conference on Friday, 20 November 2026. His remarks raise a central legal question: can a president impose such a charge without approval from Congress?
The comments followed the administration's efforts to expand American AI infrastructure. Trump argued that companies should build data centres in the United States rather than overseas, but he gave no proposed tax rate, implementation date or details about how the penalty would operate.
He also suggested the announcement was new even to members of his administration. 'I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people,' Trump told reporters. His remarks outlined an intention, not an enacted tax or formal policy.
Trump AI Data Center Tax Faces Questions Over Legal Authority
Article I, Section 8 of the US Constitution gives Congress the power to levy and collect federal taxes. The president does not have an independent constitutional power to create a new tax, although Congress can delegate specific authorities to the executive branch through legislation.
Trump did not identify any statute that would authorise the threatened charge. Without a legal basis, his announcement alone cannot create a tax obligation for companies investing in overseas data centres.
The distinction matters because Trump did not explain whether he envisaged a corporate tax, a tariff or another form of penalty. Each approach would raise different legal questions, including which activities would trigger payment and which government agency could enforce the measure.
Tariffs generally apply to imported goods. A data centre built in Finland is not itself an imported product simply because its owner is an American company. A charge on US businesses for investing in overseas infrastructure would therefore require a legal mechanism specifically capable of reaching that activity.
The Supreme Court's 2026 decision in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump also held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorise the president to impose tariffs. That ruling does not resolve every possible legal route for a data-centre penalty, but it limits the use of that particular emergency-powers law as a basis for imposing tariffs.
Trump also said the United States would not allow American companies to build data centres in other countries. Restricting overseas investment would be a separate intervention from taxing it and would likewise require a valid legal basis.
Google's Finland Investment Puts Trump AI Data Center Tax in Focus
Finland is relevant to the debate because Trump referred to overseas data-centre construction. Google already operates a facility in Hamina and announced in September that it would invest €13 billion across Finland over the following two years.
Google said the commitment would support digital infrastructure, clean energy projects and local economic partnerships. It is not exclusively a budget for building data centres. Trump did not identify Google as a target of his proposal or explain whether existing projects would be affected.
For technology companies, overseas facilities can help serve customers in different markets. Proximity to users can reduce delays in data processing, while local data requirements, electricity availability and operating costs can influence where infrastructure is developed. An international project does not necessarily replace investment in the United States.
Domestic expansion also faces planning and regulatory challenges. Loudoun County, Virginia, announced on 18 November that its Board of Supervisors had voted to pause final action on certain data-centre and electrical-substation applications for up to 12 months.
The local decision illustrates the planning challenges facing domestic infrastructure projects, even as the administration encourages companies to build more facilities in the United States.
For technology companies with overseas expansion plans, the immediate uncertainty is how the administration might attempt to implement Trump's threat. Until the White House produces a formal proposal or identifies an existing statutory authority, businesses cannot determine which investments could be affected or whether the measure would withstand legal scrutiny.
Trump's AI Data Centre Tax Threat Divides Online Opinion
Online reactions to Trump's remarks reflected differing views about the economic and technological consequences of restricting overseas data centre development.
One commenter supported Trump's position, arguing that overseas investment could cost the United States jobs, revenue and control over sensitive information.
'I think what he said is correct. Losing data centers to overseas will result in loss of investment and income within the United States. It will also create data security issues. The United States has vast land and can totally build them in remote areas,' the commenter wrote.
Others questioned whether Trump's approach could undermine America's competitiveness in artificial intelligence.
'At this time, just come out and say no more data centers period. Congrats China, you win,' another commenter wrote.
A third raised concerns that uncertainty over data centre development could delay construction and further affect an already struggling industry.
'So data centers won't be built anywhere for a long time...not good for an already suffering AI industry...,' the commenter wrote.

sources.news_title: Trump threatens a 'tremendous tax' on tech companies building data centers outside the US
sources.text:
Donald Trump gave a stark warning to companies looking to build data centers overseas.
Trump said at Friday's White House press briefing that his administration would impose a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centers outside the US, adding that "China will take all of them."
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said. "We're not going to allow that to happen."
Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI have backed data-center projects outside the United States. Companies often build abroad to serve regional users, meet local data requirements, improve reliability, or secure available power and land while avoiding battles at home.
"We want them to build it here. If they won't go in Texas or they won't go in California, they're going to go in West Virginia," Trump added. "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places."
Across the country, Americans have raised concerns at town halls and in local fights over data-center projects that the facilities could drive up electricity bills, create pollution, and strain power grids.
Trump also urged local governments to work with data center builders.
"You have to take advantage of the data centers," Trump said, addressing local representatives. "Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage; don't shut them off."
Trump returned to Washington on Thursday after a trip to China, where he met with Xi Jinping, China's leader, in Shenzhen, a major technology hub. Trump said they discussed AI development and agreed to work together on AI guardrails.

sources.news_title: Trump threatens tax for overseas US data centres
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump threatened to impose a "tremendous tax" on US companies that build their data centres overseas.
Mr Trump made the comments in a wide-ranging press conference in Washington, DC following the trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China.
"We're not going to allow companies to build data centres in other countries. If they do that, they can. But we're going to put a tremendous tax on them," Mr Trump told the media.
"China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
Data centres accounted for 23% of total metered electricity consumption in Ireland in 2025. Just under 5% of all Irish job postings on the Indeed hiring platform mention data centres, according to figures from the employment website.
On Monday, the US government moved to close a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.
The new export controls require data centres anywhere in the world to have a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other territories under US embargoes.
The breakneck development of AI technology depends heavily on the construction of large electricity-hungry data centres, which have sparked political backlash in communities across the US.
The data centres have pushed electricity rates higher, emit air pollution and consume vast amounts of water.
Mr Trump cautioned that any slowdown in data centre construction in the US would impact its lead in AI, which his administration refers to as Super Intelligence (SI).
"Whoever wins SI, wins. And you want to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community," he said.
"But take advantage. Don't shut them off."
Trump calls for 'second chance' for Huang
Mr Trump called for chipmaker Nvidia to reinstate disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang after he resigned over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
"I would love to see him be back. You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?" Mr Trump told reporters.
"I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance."
Mr Huang resigned last week as chief of Nvidia, a company at the centre of the AI revolution, after revelations of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funnelled restricted chips to that country.
Reports of at least two further affairs emerged after that initial report, with US intelligence said to be aware of the possibility of the alleged Chinese espionage.
Mr Trump defended Mr Huang as "a good man" who "made some bad decisions".
"I'd like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back because he created something with Blackwell," he said, referring to the most advanced chips designed by Nvidia.
Mr Trump also appeared to directly contradict his US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, saying he had spoken to Mr Xi about the former Nvidia CEO during a summit earlier this week.
"I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man'," he said.
Mr Bessent had earlier said that Mr Trump had not discussed Mr Huang with the Chinese president during the meeting in Shenzhen.
Mr Trump said today he is unsure if doing away with nuclear weapons "can ever happen" after meeting the leaders of Russia and China, the world's other two main nuclear powers.
"If somebody comes (and says), 'I'll make you a deal. Let's all cut them in half', it's hard to say yes, especially when you're leading," Mr Trump said. He added that it is "very, very difficult to say, 'Let's get rid of our nuclear weapons'".
Mr Trump also hailed his "fantastic relationships" with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, saying the personal ties help keep the US secure.
"I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That's a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That's a good thing, and our country is safe because of that," Mr Trump said.

sources.news_title: Trump says he'll penalize U.S. companies that build data centers in other countries
sources.text:
Trump says he’ll penalize U.S. companies that build data centers in other countries
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Americans remain rattled by a series of outages that have disrupted air travel, email services and bank transactions.
- Trump told reporters that Nvidia should give a second chance to its co-founder Jensen Huang.
- He praised his relationship with Putin but demurred when asked if Putin is a friend of the United States.
WASHINGTON — President Trump on Friday vowed to punish American companies that build data centers abroad, threatening to levy “tremendous penalties” on any that try, as he returned from Asia eager to project confidence in his push to win the global race for dominance in artificial intelligence.
“We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen,” Trump said during a sprawling news conference at the White House.
The threat was Trump’s latest bid to tighten his grip on a booming industry that has become central to the U.S. economy, and to show how America plans to set the pace in the AI race. The United States is leading, he said, China is second, and “there really is no third place.”
It was also part of a broader effort to sell what Trump called a “consequential trip” to the Philippines and China, one that ended with an unprecedented gathering with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“It was big. It was great, great electricity,” Trump said. “The relationship was fantastic between the three of us.”
The summit served to generate further angst and distrust across Asia and Europe, with several leaders publicly recoiling at Trump’s overtures of affection.
While the summit produced few tangible plans, Trump said he and Xi agreed to do “some joint guardrails” on artificial intelligence, but did not offer specifics. And in a window into how Trump sees the influence of tech giants in the AI race, Trump told reporters that he thinks Nvidia should reinstate its co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned last week amid a scandal involving an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
“He is a man who made some bad decisions but he is a brilliant person,” Trump said. “We have to protect our brilliant people … and Jensen is one of them.”
Trump’s remarks came on a turbulent day for the industry, as a sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks dragged the S&P 500 down 3.7% on Friday. It was the steepest weekly loss in more than 18 months, showing unease among investors. The drop came amid the scandal at Nvidia, and Anthropic making its debut on the public market.
Trump’s defense of the AI industry was among a medley of subjects the president addressed during a 87-minute news conference that included Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Stephen Miller, his new chief of staff.
As Cabinet members looked on, Trump praised his relationship with Putin, but when asked whether the Russian leader was a friend to the United States, he demurred, saying, “I can’t speak to America.” He also claimed that Putin told him Russia would never have invaded Ukraine in 2022 had Trump been president.
“Actually, I asked him. I said, ‘Would you have gone in if I was president?’ He said, ‘No, would have never happened.’ Trump said. “It was handled so bad by our country.”
Trump also renewed his criticism of the International Criminal Court, calling it a “fake power” that thinks it can “arrests heads of countries for no reason.” He said that he, Putin and Xi had condemned the court as a group. The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest, accusing him of war crimes over the deportation of Ukrainina children.
Trump’s news conference came as Americans remain rattled by a series of outages that have disrupted air travel, email services and bank transactions in the last week.
Asked whether there is cause for concern, Trump said the disruptions were “all separate events,” and not part of a coordinated effort.
He said nationwide ground stop was due to an “ancient” air traffic control system, but insisted it is “very safe,” and that if there was a silver lining to the technical issues the FAA experienced it is that Congress has become receptive to modernizing the system.
Trump attributed the outages at private companies, including major banks and airlines, to routine technological upgrades.
“We have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen,” he said.
But the disruptions have also raised questions about the administration’s own cybersecurity leadership after Trump fired Sean Cairncross, the national cyber director on Thursday. When asked why, Trump said: “Because I didn’t think that person was good enough.” He has tapped Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, to fill the post.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would open the door for new transmission lines, pipelines and renewables in California and across the nation.
Trump, however, brushed aside questions about tensions between him and Vance.
Asked whether he was frustrated with his vice president after he blamed Republicans’ midterm losses on the war with Iran, Trump said he never said he was “unhappy” with his stance, just that he should have clarified that he agreed with the decision to launch the war if he had to go back in time and do it again knowing the political risks.
As Vance stood behind Trump, he was asked whether he believes the war had been worth the political fallout. He told reporters his job was to support the president, and the decision has been Trump’s to make to ensure Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
With Democrats ready to take control of Congress in January, Trump signaled that he is open to working with them on legislation. He pointed to a federal tax credit for film and television production as one possible area of agreement.
“It has unbelievable support. I’ll tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill,’” Trump said of the Democratic senator from California.
In a statement, Schiff said the proposal will create jobs and boost local economies, and achieve the long-sought goal for many in Hollywood of bringing production back to the U.S.
“Given the support from the president and Republicans and Democrats in both chambers, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.
On other legislative issues, Trump said he would not hesitate to use his veto power, calling it an “extreme power” he can wield to exert control over negotiations. Still, he rejected the idea that the midterms had been a verdict on his presidency and agenda.
“I wasn’t on the ballot,” he said. “I hope you remember that.”
Times staff writer Justine McDaniel, in Washington, contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Trump threatens to penalize U.S. tech companies that build AI data centres in other countries
Trump threatens data-center tax on American companies building abroad - FINCHANNEL
sources.text:
The FINANCIAL — President Donald Trump threatened a data-center tax on American companies building facilities overseas on Friday, November 20, proposing penalties for a business whose largest operators already maintain international networks serving customers outside the United States.
Speaking at a White House news conference after his trip to Asia, Trump said he wanted to prevent American companies from building data centers abroad and would impose a large tax if they did. He presented the proposal as a way to help the American artificial intelligence industry compete with China, according to Reuters’ report on his remarks.
The announcement came without details of how the policy would operate. The Associated Press reported that Trump said he had not yet told his own officials about the plan.
Trump also urged American communities to welcome data centers and negotiate payments or other benefits from their developers. His appeal addressed a separate obstacle facing domestic construction: opposition from places being asked to accommodate the buildings and their demands on local infrastructure.
The AP reported that technology companies were responding to such resistance with promises involving fewer taxpayer subsidies, greater disclosure or more spending in host communities. Friday’s remarks set out the president’s preferred direction, while leaving the proposed overseas penalty’s implementation unresolved.
Reuters identified Equinix and Digital Realty among American developers operating abroad. Facilities are often located close to users to reduce delays for tasks such as processing payments, the news agency reported, while sending large quantities of data over long distances can add costs.
Overseas commitments already announced
Amazon’s March 2 announcement in Spain described plans to invest €33.7 billion in cloud and AI infrastructure, adding €18 billion to a previously announced €15.7 billion commitment. Its AWS Europe region in Aragón opened in November 2022.
The company said the expansion would include facilities supporting its data-center supply chain: a plant for server assembly and testing, a manufacturing fulfillment warehouse, and an AI and machine-learning server manufacturing and repair facility. Amazon projected about 1,800 jobs at those facilities once fully operational.
Amazon also announced plans for €30 million in Spanish community programs through 2035, covering education, sustainability, social impact and local development. These were company commitments announced months before Trump’s remarks, rather than a response to Friday’s proposal.
Amazon estimated that the Spanish investment would support 29,900 full-time-equivalent jobs annually in local businesses, including direct, indirect and induced employment. It projected a €31.7 billion contribution to Spain’s gross domestic product through 2035. These are company forecasts.
In Germany, Amazon announced on October 20 that it planned to invest more than €16 billion in 2027 across several businesses. That total includes logistics, satellite connectivity and entertainment as well as cloud infrastructure.
The cloud-specific component is €4.8 billion for expanding the AWS Europe region in Frankfurt in 2027. Amazon said the money would help meet demand for cloud and AI services; the entire German investment total is not a data-center construction budget.
The Frankfurt region opened in October 2014. Amazon’s German announcement also referred to its European Sovereign Cloud, which became generally available in January 2026, and to data-center apprenticeships offered with Siemens since 2023.
Why cloud companies build locally
AWS’s January 15 launch announcement described the European Sovereign Cloud as entirely located within the European Union and physically and logically separate from its other cloud regions. The company said the service was designed for governments and businesses with sensitive-data requirements.
AWS also announced plans for additional Local Zones in Belgium, the Netherlands and Portugal. These facilities allow customers to keep data in a particular location or run applications sensitive to delays, according to the company.
The company said its European service would be operated by EU residents and would have no critical dependence on infrastructure outside the bloc. Those are AWS’s descriptions of its operating design and safeguards. Its announcement framed the expansion around customers’ demands for data residency, operational independence and access to cloud services.
Limited space in established markets
The commercial property firm CBRE’s June 17 report documented tight availability in major American data-center markets even as new capacity was added. Its figures describe the first quarter of 2026, rather than conditions measured on the day of Trump’s announcement.
Across Northern Virginia, Atlanta, Dallas-Fort Worth and Chicago, inventory increased 33 percent from a year earlier. Northern Virginia’s vacancy rate was 0.3 percent, compared with 1 percent in Atlanta, 1.8 percent in Dallas-Fort Worth and 2.2 percent in Chicago.
CBRE reported that power availability and grid constraints were affecting development schedules and location decisions in established American and European hubs. It also identified local opposition as a constraint on supply. In Europe’s four largest markets—London, Frankfurt, Paris and Amsterdam—inventory grew 18.9 percent from a year earlier.
Electricity forecasts show a wide range
A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study published in June 2026 estimated that American data centers could use 649 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2030 under its reference case, equivalent to 11.8 percent of total U.S. electricity use.
The study, titled the United States Data Center Energy Usage Report: 2025 Update, presented a wider combined uncertainty range of 521 to 843 terawatt-hours. That corresponds to between 9.5 percent and 15.3 percent of U.S. electricity use in 2030.
Its model builds estimates from equipment shipments, electricity use per device and cooling-system performance. Alternative scenarios change assumptions about equipment installations, specialized graphics chips, chip lifetimes and server utilization. The results are forecasts under different assumptions, not measured consumption for 2030 or estimates of the effects of Trump’s proposed penalty.
The International Energy Agency’s 2026 report, Key Questions on Energy and AI, estimated that global data-center electricity demand increased 17 percent in 2025. Consumption at AI-focused facilities rose faster, increasing 50 percent.
The agency projected that total data-center consumption would roughly double from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 terawatt-hours in 2030, reaching about 3 percent of global electricity demand. AI-focused data-center consumption was projected to triple over that period.
The IEA identified competing forces shaping that outlook: efficiency improvements, increased use of AI and the adoption of more energy-intensive applications. Video generation, reasoning and agentic tasks can require far more energy per query than simple text generation, it said. The agency also identified financing conditions and expectations for investment returns as factors influencing the pace of construction.
Governments confront connection queues
In its October report, Powering Artificial Intelligence, the IEA examined more than 34 policy jurisdictions covering about 90 percent of global data-center capacity. It identified 134 policies and regulations governing how data centers integrate with electricity systems, with nearly 40 percent announced or implemented in the preceding year.
The report cautioned that connection queues include speculative or duplicate projects. Overestimating demand can leave grid investments underused, while underestimating it can produce delays and bottlenecks.
Operators signed renewable-electricity purchase agreements covering 45 terawatt-hours in the first half of 2026, nearly 20 percent more than a year earlier, the agency said. Nearly 70 percent of that contracted volume was in the United States.
The IEA estimated that the largest data-center operators would spend more than $700 billion in capital expenditure in 2026, mostly on new data centers. It cited Texas, Virginia, Finland and the United Kingdom among places with large connection queues.
FAQ
Did Trump announce an operating tax system?
He announced his intention to penalize overseas construction. The AP reported that he provided no implementation details and said he had not yet informed his officials.
Are the U.S. electricity figures actual consumption?
No. The laboratory’s 2030 figures are model-based projections, with a reference case and an uncertainty range reflecting different assumptions about equipment and electricity use.

U.S. technology companies could face steep financial penalties if they build artificial intelligence data centers outside the country. President Donald Trump announced the threat Friday, arguing that overseas construction could give China greater access to critical computing infrastructure.

Companies such as Equinix and Digital Realty already develop and operate data centers outside the United States. Major American technology companies, including Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta, also maintain international computing operations supporting their global businesses.
Data centers house servers, networking equipment and other infrastructure required to process and store large volumes of information. They have become increasingly important as technology companies develop more advanced artificial intelligence systems requiring substantial computing capacity.
Many companies establish facilities in foreign markets to serve regional customers, reduce delays in data processing and comply with local data storage requirements. Locating infrastructure near users can also reduce the expense of transmitting large quantities of information across international networks.
Restrictions on overseas development could therefore affect existing business strategies, international technology investments and the ability of American companies to compete in foreign markets.
Trump’s proposal reflects a broader administration effort to maintain American leadership in artificial intelligence while limiting China’s access to advanced U.S. computing technology.
The federal government has already imposed restrictions on exports of sophisticated artificial intelligence chips to China over concerns that the technology could strengthen Beijing’s military and intelligence capabilities.
Earlier this week, the Commerce Department moved to tighten restrictions on advanced chip exports to several Southeast Asian countries, seeking to prevent Chinese companies from obtaining American technology through third-party destinations.
Chinese businesses have reportedly gained access to advanced computing capabilities by renting processing capacity from data centers located in countries permitted to import American chips.
The arrangement has raised questions about whether existing export controls adequately prevent restricted technology from supporting Chinese artificial intelligence development.
Trump’s proposed penalties would represent a different approach by targeting the location of computing facilities operated by American businesses, rather than focusing exclusively on individual semiconductor exports.
The announcement also comes amid growing opposition to data center construction within the United States, where communities have raised concerns about electricity consumption, rising utility expenses, water usage and the effect of large industrial facilities on surrounding neighborhoods.
Despite those objections, Trump has repeatedly encouraged Americans to support domestic data center development, arguing that the facilities create economic opportunities and strengthen national security.
“We’re going to fight very hard for the data centers,” Trump said during Friday’s appearance.
The president urged communities to negotiate financial benefits from companies seeking to construct facilities rather than oppose the projects outright.
“You ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” Trump said, according to Associated Press reporting on the announcement.
The administration has previously encouraged major technology companies to assume responsibility for the electricity and infrastructure costs associated with new data centers.
Under the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, participating companies commit to paying the full cost of energy generation and infrastructure required for their facilities rather than passing those expenses to residential electricity customers.
The pledge is intended to address concerns that rapidly expanding artificial intelligence operations could increase household utility bills as demand for electricity grows.
However, local opposition remains substantial. An August survey by the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center found that 61% of Americans were somewhat or strongly opposed to new data centers being constructed near their homes, compared with 49% several months earlier.
According to The Washington Post’s report on Trump’s announcement, the president’s latest proposal introduces uncertainty for technology companies already pursuing international expansion while attempting to respond to growing resistance to domestic construction.
The debate intensified during the November midterm elections, when concerns about the environmental and financial effects of artificial intelligence infrastructure became a significant issue in several communities.
Some technology companies have responded by pledging greater transparency about proposed projects, offering financial benefits to local governments and agreeing to cover additional infrastructure expenses.
Microsoft has also announced that it will stop seeking certain local tax incentives for new data center developments, reflecting efforts to address criticism over the public costs associated with the industry.
Trump’s proposal comes as federal lawmakers consider separate legislation designed to accelerate domestic energy and infrastructure construction.
The Senate approved bipartisan permitting reform legislation Thursday intended to shorten federal approval timelines for major energy projects. The measure also includes provisions addressing the allocation of electricity infrastructure expenses associated with large data centers.
Supporters argue that faster construction of power generation and transmission infrastructure could help the United States accommodate rising electricity demand while remaining competitive in artificial intelligence development.
However, the president’s proposed overseas tax raises separate legal and economic questions.
Congress generally controls federal taxation, and imposing a new tax specifically targeting companies based on the location of their overseas data centers could require legislation or another legally authorized mechanism.
The administration has not explained whether the threatened penalties would apply to new projects, existing investments or companies that provide computing services through foreign subsidiaries.
It also remains unclear whether the restrictions would distinguish between artificial intelligence training facilities and conventional data centers used for cloud computing, banking transactions, telecommunications and other commercial services.
Those distinctions could significantly affect the scope of any future policy because American technology companies depend on geographically distributed infrastructure to support customers in multiple countries.
The president’s announcement has not yet resulted in a formal tax or prohibition on constructing data centers abroad.
For now, the proposal signals the administration’s intention to keep advanced computing investment within the United States while expanding restrictions intended to prevent China from accessing American-developed artificial intelligence capabilities.
Whether the White House can implement the threatened penalties, and how the technology industry responds, will depend on the legal framework and specific requirements established in any subsequent policy.

sources.news_title: Trump threatens penalties on US companies building data centers abroad
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Friday threatened “a tremendous tax” on U.S. companies that build artificial intelligence data centers abroad, highlighting a divide between a president who sees their expansion as critical to winning the AI race and an American public that is deeply skeptical of their benefits.
Briefing reporters at the White House shortly after his return from Asia, the president said the country was ahead of China in developing what he likes to call “super intelligence.” But he warned it could fall behind if a growing political backlash puts the brakes on development of the data centers that are driving the AI boom.
“We’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries,” the president said. “If they do that, they can. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.”
He contrasted his push to keep AI infrastructure in the U.S. with the foreign production of advanced computer chips, which he said had been “very destructive to our country.”
Trump said he had not yet told his staff about his proposal to target data center development outside the U.S., and it was not immediately clear how it would be enforced.
His statements emphasized the gap between Trump’s view of AI development and the views of most Americans and came less than three weeks after voter concerns about data centers contributed to a Republican wipe-out in the midterm elections.
About three-quarters of U.S. voters in this year’s election said they opposed the construction of a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll.
In a survey taken over the summer, about 6 in 10 Americans said they supported limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans, according to the poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago.
The same survey found that a majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.
With Democrats winning large majorities in both houses of Congress, a tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.
He suggested that data center concerns could be addressed through community negotiations with the tech companies seeking to build them. Tax breaks, reduced utility bills, money for teachers, direct payments to local residents all could be part of the talks.
“Make the deal,” Trump said. “They have plenty of money. Take it.”
The development of artificial intelligence is an important growth factor for data centers, but cloud computing services remain the dominant use of data centers in the U.S., industry officials say.
With host communities across the U.S. turning against the gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets and shower more money on communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
Besides ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.
Companies also are making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining that AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics.
“We want them to build it here,” Trump said.
Many of the tech giants already have global footprints. Google has data centers in Asia and Europe.
Trump’s threat to penalize companies that build data centers overseas reflects his view that the buildout is a boon for the U.S. economy. Most economists agree, but with caveats.
The largest high-tech firms are projected to spend as much as $1.8 trillion next year developing AI, mostly on data centers, economists at UBS estimate. The buildup has also boosted wages for some construction workers, particularly skilled contractors such as electricians, who are in short supply.
At the same time, most of the goods that power data centers — particularly semiconductors, but also materials such as copper — are imported, which offsets much of the economic gain.
On Thursday, the Republican-led Senate approved bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting reviews for power plants, transmission lines, and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and to lower electricity prices.
The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use and upgrades to the larger transmission network.
Trump praised the Senate bill, which now goes to the House: “It’s going to cause tremendous amounts of new building,” he said.

Cooper reported from Phoenix. Associated Press writer Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and business writer Christopher Rugaber in Washington contributed to this report.

“We’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries,” the president said. “If they do that, they can. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.”
He contrasted his push to keep AI infrastructure in the U.S. with the foreign production of advanced computer chips, which he said had been “very destructive to our country.”
Trump said he had not yet told his staff about his proposal to target data center development outside the U.S., and it was not immediately clear how it would be enforced.
His statements emphasized the gap between Trump’s view of AI development and the views of most Americans and came less than three weeks after voter concerns about data centers contributed to a Republican wipe-out in the midterm elections.
About three-quarters of U.S. voters in this year's election said they opposed the construction of a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll.
In a survey taken over the summer, about 6 in 10 Americans said they supported limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans, according to the poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago.
The same survey found that a majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.
With Democrats winning large majorities in both houses of Congress, a tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.
He suggested that data center concerns could be addressed through community negotiations with the tech companies seeking to build them. Tax breaks, reduced utility bills, money for teachers, direct payments to local residents all could be part of the talks.
“Make the deal,” Trump said. “They have plenty of money. Take it.”
The development of artificial intelligence is an important growth factor for data centers, but cloud computing services remain the dominant use of data centers in the U.S., industry officials say.
With host communities across the U.S. turning against the gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets and shower more money on communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
Besides ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.
Companies also are making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining that AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics.
“We want them to build it here,” Trump said.
Many of the tech giants already have global footprints. Google has data centers in Asia and Europe.
Trump’s threat to penalize companies that build data centers overseas reflects his view that the buildout is a boon for the U.S. economy. Most economists agree, but with caveats.
The largest high-tech firms are projected to spend as much as $1.8 trillion next year developing AI, mostly on data centers, economists at UBS estimate. The buildup has also boosted wages for some construction workers, particularly skilled contractors such as electricians, who are in short supply.
At the same time, most of the goods that power data centers — particularly semiconductors, but also materials such as copper — are imported, which offsets much of the economic gain.
On Thursday, the Republican-led Senate approved bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting reviews for power plants, transmission lines, and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and to lower electricity prices.
The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use and upgrades to the larger transmission network.
Trump praised the Senate bill, which now goes to the House: “It’s going to cause tremendous amounts of new building,” he said.

Trump says he’ll penalize US companies that build data centers in other countries
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Friday vowed to punish American companies that build data centers abroad, threatening to levy “tremendous penalties” on any that try, as he returned from Asia eager to project confidence in his push to win the global race for dominance in artificial intelligence.
“We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen,” Trump said during a sprawling news conference at the White House.
The threat was Trump’s latest bid to tighten his grip on a booming industry that has become central to the U.S. economy, and to show how America plans to set the pace in the AI race. The United States is leading, he said, China is second, and “there really is no third place.”
It was also part of a broader effort to sell what Trump called a “consequential trip” to the Philippines and China, one that ended with an unprecedented gathering with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“It was big. It was great, great electricity,” Trump said. “The relationship was fantastic between the three of us.”
While the summit produced few tangible plans, Trump said he and Xi agreed to do “some joint guardrails” on artificial intelligence, but did not offer specifics. And in a window into how Trump sees the influence of tech giants in the AI race, Trump told reporters that he thinks Nvidia should reinstate its co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned last week amid a scandal involving an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
“He is a man who made some bad decisions but he is a brilliant person,” Trump said. “We have to protect our brilliant people … and Jensen is one of them.”
Trump’s remarks came on a turbulent day for the industry, as a sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks dragged the S&P 500 down 3.7% on Friday. It was the steepest weekly loss in more than 18 months, showing unease among investors. The drop came amid the scandal at Nvidia, and Anthropic making its debut on the public market.
Trump’s defense of the AI industry was among a medley of subjects the president addressed during a 87-minute news conference that included Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Stephen Miller, his new chief of staff.
As Cabinet members looked on, Trump praised his relationship with Putin, but when asked whether the Russian leader was a friend to the United States, he demurred, saying, “I can’t speak to America.” He also claimed that Putin told him Russia would never have invaded Ukraine in 2022 had Trump been president.
“Actually, I asked him. I said, ‘Would you have gone in if I was president?’ He said, ‘No, would have never happened.’ Trump said. “It was handled so bad by our country.”
Trump also renewed his criticism of the International Criminal Court, calling it a “fake power” that thinks it can “arrests heads of countries for no reason.” He said that he, Putin and Xi had condemned the court as a group. The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest, accusing him of war crimes over the deportation of Ukrainian children.
Trump’s news conference came as Americans remain rattled by a series of outages that have disrupted air travel, email services and bank transactions in the last week.
Asked whether there is cause for concern, Trump said the disruptions were “all separate events,” and not part of a coordinated effort.
He said nationwide ground stop was due to an “ancient” air traffic control system, but insisted it is “very safe,” and that if there was a silver lining to the technical issues the FAA experienced it is that Congress has become receptive to modernizing the system.
Trump attributed the outages at private companies, including major banks and airlines, to routine technological upgrades.
“We have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen,” he said.
But the disruptions have also raised questions about the administration’s own cybersecurity leadership after Trump fired Sean Cairncross, the national cyber director on Thursday. When asked why, Trump said: “Because I didn’t think that person was good enough.” He has tapped Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, to fill the post.
Trump, however, brushed aside questions about tensions between him and Vance.
Asked whether he was frustrated with his vice president after he blamed Republicans’ midterm losses on the war with Iran, Trump said he never said he was “unhappy” with his stance, just that he should have clarified that he agreed with the decision to launch the war if he had to go back in time and do it again knowing the political risks.
As Vance stood behind Trump, he was asked whether he believes the war had been worth the political fallout. He told reporters his job was to support the president, and the decision has been Trump’s to make to ensure Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
With Democrats ready to take control of Congress in January, Trump signaled that he is open to working with them on legislation. He pointed to a federal tax credit for film and television production as one possible area of agreement.
“It has unbelievable support. I’ll tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill,’” Trump said of the Democratic senator from California.
In a statement, Schiff said the proposal will create jobs and boost local economies, and achieve the long-sought goal for many in Hollywood of bringing production back to the U.S.
“Given the support from the president and Republicans and Democrats in both chambers, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.
On other legislative issues, Trump said he would not hesitate to use his veto power, calling it an “extreme power” he can wield to exert control over negotiations. Still, he rejected the idea that the midterms had been a verdict on his presidency and agenda.
“I wasn’t on the ballot,” he said. “I hope you remember that.”
—Los Angeles Times staff writer Justine McDaniel, in Washington, contributed to this report.

Trump Threatens a Tax on US Firms That Build Data Centres Abroad
Donald Trump said the United States would penalise American companies that build data centres overseas, promising a tremendous tax on any that do, and framed the move as a way to help the country's AI industry compete with China. He said the US would not allow its companies to build data centres outside the country.
The policy lands on companies with large overseas footprints. Equinix and Digital Realty both build and operate facilities well beyond the United States, and the industry's reason for doing so is physical rather than political, since servers sit close to users to cut the delay on time sensitive work such as payment processing, and shipping large volumes of data over long distances carries its own cost.
And no mechanism exists yet. Trump gave no rate, no draft rule and no date in the briefing after his Asia trip, so what a tremendous tax means in practice, and whether it would apply to construction, operation or both, is unknown.
The domestic politics are simpler than the economics. Data centres have drawn opposition across American communities over electricity demand, utility bills and local disruption, and Trump has been a strong advocate of building them at home, a position that puts him on both sides of a popular complaint.
The timing fits a wider squeeze. The Commerce Department moved this week to require licences for advanced AI chip exports to several South-east Asian countries, adding Singapore to a list of places where American silicon now needs permission to land, part of an effort to stop China obtaining the technology through third countries.
And the loophole it targets is real. The US already bars direct sales of its most advanced chips to China, yet Chinese firms have kept access by renting computing capacity at data centres in countries that can legally import the hardware, which is why where a data centre sits has become a security question rather than a commercial one.
For Asia the consequence is a threat to the model that has driven the region's buildout. Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and India have all courted American operators on the promise of capacity and jobs, and a penalty on building abroad would make each of those projects a question for a treasury department rather than a planning committee.

U.S. President Donald Trump threatened on Friday, November 20, to impose a “tremendous tax” on American technology companies establishing artificial intelligence data centres overseas, as growing opposition to large-scale AI infrastructure projects raises concerns about investment leaving the United States.
The warning follows the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, during which concerns about rising electricity costs, water consumption and pressure on local power grids became major issues in communities hosting or considering new data centres. The incoming Democratic-controlled Congress, scheduled to convene on January 3, 2027, could bring greater scrutiny of the industry’s energy demands, environmental impact and infrastructure costs.
Trump has not specified the proposed tax rate or explained how such a measure would be implemented. However, his administration has emphasized expanding domestic AI infrastructure as a central economic and national security priority, seeking to maintain American technological leadership over China. The prospect of stricter regulations and prolonged approval processes could encourage technology companies to consider alternative locations in Canada, Europe and Asia.
AI data centres are capital-intensive facilities equipped with specialized computer chips, servers and cooling systems used to train and operate artificial intelligence models. Major technology companies, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, invest billions of dollars in these facilities, generating revenue through cloud computing services, AI subscriptions and enterprise technology platforms. Large developments can cost between $5 billion and $13 billion or more, with electricity requirements comparable to those of small cities.
Alberta has emerged as a potential beneficiary of the industry’s expansion, with the provincial government seeking approximately $100 billion in data centre investment over five years. Among the developments described in industry proposals is a $13 billion Meta-linked project in Sturgeon County, north of Edmonton. Alberta’s appeal includes its natural gas resources, available land and potential for dedicated electricity generation, although the province is also considering restrictions on where facilities can be built.
For governments, the economic benefits extend beyond construction spending. Large data centres can generate municipal property taxes, provincial corporate taxes, equipment-related levies and natural gas royalties where gas-fired electricity generation is involved. Estimates cited for a one-gigawatt Alberta development suggest potential combined public revenues of approximately $250 million annually, including around $40 million in municipal property taxes. Such projections depend on the facility’s ownership, energy supply, assessment rules and applicable taxes.
However, the employment benefits are less extensive once construction ends. A major facility could support approximately 3,000 construction jobs but require only around 300 permanent employees. Critics also question whether the resulting tax revenues adequately compensate communities for increased electricity demand, water consumption and infrastructure requirements.
The debate presents a significant challenge for Trump’s economic agenda. His administration has promoted artificial intelligence investment as a defining element of American industrial competitiveness, but opposition to data centre construction threatens to slow domestic expansion. A punitive tax on overseas development could discourage companies from relocating projects, although it would not necessarily resolve the energy shortages, regulatory disputes and local resistance driving their decisions.
For Canada, particularly Alberta, the outcome could influence billions of dollars in prospective technology investment. For Washington, the challenge is balancing Trump’s ambition to secure American AI leadership with mounting public pressure to ensure that the industry’s rapid growth does not impose excessive costs on households and local communities.

sources.news_title: Yet Another Open Letter to Donald Trump
sources.text:
Mr. Donald J. Trump
President, Executive Branch
United States Government
Washington, DC
Mr. Trump:
CNBC reports that you plan either to prohibit American companies from building data centers abroad or to impose a “tremendous tax” on those that do (“Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatens ‘tremendous tax’,” November 20). You obviously believe that America loses when Americans invest abroad. Yet you also insist that America loses when it runs trade deficits. These two beliefs are inconsistent.
This inconsistency isn’t ideological. It’s accounting. America’s trade deficits are mirrored by surpluses in its capital account. These surpluses arise because foreigners invest more in America than Americans invest abroad. The greater the excess of foreign investment in America over American investment abroad, the larger are America’s trade (or current-account) deficits. And, hence, the more Americans invest abroad, all other things equal, the smaller are U.S. trade deficits. By discouraging Americans from investing abroad, you therefore discourage an activity that reduces America’s trade deficits.
You regularly boast, moreover, about the “trillions” of dollars of foreign investment that you claim your trade policies are drawing into America. Yet each additional dollar of foreign investment in America, other things equal, increases America’s trade deficits. You thus celebrate foreign investment in the U.S. which enlarges U.S. trade deficits while proposing to punish American investment abroad which helps shrink these deficits. You applaud and promote activities that raise U.S. trade deficits while condemning and punishing activities that shrink these deficits.
Unlike you, I don’t regard trade deficits as evidence of economic weakness, or trade surpluses as evidence of economic strength. Both reflect the investment decisions of people around the world. But given your incessant insistence that trade deficits harm America, you can’t sensibly discourage American investment abroad while celebrating foreign investment here. Both policies push the trade deficit in the direction that you deplore.
You can wage war against American investment abroad, or you can wage war against America’s trade deficits. But accounting makes certain that you cannot consistently wage both wars.
Sincerely,
Donald J. Boudreaux
Professor of Economics
and
Martha and Nelson Getchell Chair for the Study of Free Market Capitalism at the Mercatus Center
George Mason University
Fairfax, VA 22030

sources.news_title: Trump Plans to Penalize U.S. Tech Firms Building AI Centers Abroad
sources.text:
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump said U.S. technology companies could face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers overseas.
Trump offered no specifics Friday and acknowledged that he had not yet briefed his own administration officials on the proposal. The Republican president also encouraged Americans to welcome data center projects in their communities while pressing developers for concessions, a position he raised before the midterm elections.
Trump said, “You ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off.”
As communities around the country push back against massive data centers, the nation’s technology giants are offering new assurances. They are pledging to seek fewer taxpayer subsidies, operate with greater transparency and direct more money to communities that agree to host the server facilities.

The latest wave of commitments from some of the world’s wealthiest companies arrived as opposition to data centers emerged as a powerful issue in the midterm elections, when Democrats won control of Congress.
Even with Trump’s support, the data centers driving the artificial intelligence boom have become politically controversial. Local resistance has stalled municipal approvals, creating a major obstacle for the industry. Technology companies could encounter further setbacks if voters next month elect additional public officials who are wary of large-scale data center development.

Trump Says U.S. Companies Will Face Ban or Tax for Overseas Data Centers
At a Nov. 20 White House press conference, he said he had not told his staff about the policy before announcing it.
President Donald Trump said Nov. 20 that U.S. companies will be barred from building data centers in other countries or face a “tremendous tax,” outlining a proposed policy that could affect firms expanding computing infrastructure overseas.
“We’re going to fight very hard for the data centers,” Trump said at a White House press conference. He said he had not told his staff about the proposal before announcing it.
Trump did not provide further policy details in his remarks.
